transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-23
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Liu (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Anika Rao (Lead ML Eng, DataForge), Carlos Mendes (Platform Eng), Jules Park (CTO)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be noisy):
- Focus: throughput tuning for bursty inferencing workloads, tradeoffs between latency and cost, KV cache prefetch strategies, token-adaptive throttling knobs (max_num_seqs, token limits) and VPC/on-prem considerations.
- Agreed to run a stress benchmark with proposed knobs and to share security and deployment docs.

Topics: continuous batching, max_num_seqs, token limits, KV prefetch, quantization impact on throughput, VPC pinning, fallbacks.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for hopping on, it's 15:30 here, we wanted to run through token-adaptive throttling ideas and a prefetch approach for your bursty API patterns.
[00:18] Anika: yeah thanks, we got notes, real quick context — we're pushing chat and completion endpoints for a customer-facing app. bursts during mornings, lots of short prompts but occasionally long summarizations. latency tail is killing conversion.
[00:36] Samir: cool, so two levers we usually tune: continuous batching plus scheduler knobs like max_num_seqs and token limits per request. combined with KV cache prewarm/prefetch we can reduce per-token cost and tail latency.
[00:50] Jules: curious about the quantization angle — we looked at 4-bit quant but worried about quality regressions for summarization.
[01:05] Samir: yeah, quantization tradeoff is model-specific. int8 or 4-bit can give 1.5-2x throughput, but you'll see subtle regen errors on long-context productions. we usually test on your eval prompts. for throughput tuning itself, quant helps but doesn't replace good scheduling.
[01:25] Carlos: when you say max_num_seqs what's the practical implication? our engineers set token caps previously and we saw tail increase.
[01:38] Samir: good question — max_num_seqs limits how many sequences can be coalesced into a single batch for a GPU go. higher gives better throughput but increases latency for new arrivals because it waits for sequences to fill. we've been experimenting with token-adaptive thresholds so small requests get fast-path and don't wait for big coalesces.
[01:58] Anika: token-adaptive? like per-client token budgets?
[02:05] Maya: more like per-request pathing: the scheduler looks at request length estimate and either routes to a low-latency lane or a high-throughput lane. the knobs are: max_num_seqs, max_tokens_per_batch, and per-client token_limit. combined with priority windows you can preserve tail latency for interactive users.
[02:27] [crosstalk]
[02:33] Carlos: okay, what's a priority window?
[02:37] Samir: a small time-window (e.g., 20-40ms) where short requests are prioritized and routed immediately; long requests are buffered to fill bigger batches. it reduces head-of-line blocking. but you need to tune eviction and token ceilings to prevent starvation.
[02:52] Anika: we have a lot of recurring prefix tokens — many prompts share the same system prompt and initial context. can KV caching help?
[03:05] Samir: absolutely. KV cache hit-rate is huge. two patterns: prefix cache (prefix/KV cache) and prefetch on warmup. for prefix-heavy workloads you should prewarm the KV cache for frequent prefixes. that reduces decoder work per request.
[03:21] Jules: so prefetching means we precompute KV states for prefixes and keep them in RAM across requests? we run in VPC with pinned GPUs so memory costs are a concern.
[03:34] Samir: yes, prefetch keeps KV in GPU or host side depending on config. there are tradeoffs: memory vs latency. our runtime supports eviction policies (LRU-ish) and TTL. if you pin a pool (Dedicated or on-prem) you can afford more prewarming. but for multi-tenant hosted we do dynamic eviction.
[03:56] Anika: how do you handle cold-cache bursts? morning spikes often hit cold.
[04:03] Samir: a few strategies: 1) prefetch top N prefixes from request traces, 2) proactive warming during expected spike windows, 3) fallback to a smaller low-latency model variant when cold to preserve tail. we also support soft-priority windows to let some requests bypass big coalesces during cold starts.
[04:23] Carlos: soft-priority windows — is that something we can do in VPC? we run a private deployment.
[04:30] Maya: yes, in Private and Dedicated you can run these knobs. in VPC mode you control autoscaler and pool pinning; we expose scheduler params in the control plane. in on-prem, you have full control over memory allocations for KV states.
[04:46] [00:04:46 - Speaker label glitch: Speaker 1]
[04:50] Speaker 1: uh I'm sorry I'm on mute — can you repeat the knob names?
[04:55] Samir: sure: max_num_seqs (max sequences per batch), batch_token_ceiling (max tokens per batch), token_limit_per_request (per-request token guard), priority_window_ms, kv_prefetch_list and kv_ttl, eviction_policy. also a continuous_batching flag - that toggles the runtime's continuous packing algorithm.
[05:21] Anika: continuous_batching — what's the main difference from simple fixed-interval batching?
[05:27] Samir: continuous batching constantly packs arrivals into in-flight kernels rather than waiting fixed micro-batches. it's better for throughput and can reduce per-token latency when traffic is steady. downside: more variability under very spiky loads if not paired with token guards.
[05:44] Carlos: under our load profile (lots of small prompts), continuous batching helped before, but we saw message ordering oddities and some timeouts. is that normal?
[05:54] Samir: timeouts usually come from long requests blocking the GPU when max_num_seqs is too high. you need to set per-request token ceiling and priority windows so short requests don't wait behind a 4000-token gen. we also recommend reactive burst scaling if you're on Dedicated.
[06:14] Jules: you mentioned quantization earlier — if we quantize the model down to 4-bit, KV cache changes?
[06:22] Samir: KV stays as floats in most implementations — but there are quantization storage strategies. some q4 implementations keep activations in reduced precision which can speed kernel ops but the cache hit/eviction logic remains similar. we need to test quality on your prompts.
[06:36] Anika: can we do an A/B where we route 10% of production to a quantized low-cost path?
[06:41] Maya: yes, rollouts are supported — canary 10%, monitor quality with evals tied to your prompt set. we can wire that up and an automatic fallback policy if quality drops.
[06:55] [00:06:55 timestamp]
[07:00] Carlos: curious about metrics — what should we watch during benchmark?
[07:03] Samir: key ones: tail latency p95/p99, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, batch size distribution, KV cache hit-rate, and evictions/sec. also monitor quality metrics for A/B.
[07:17] Anika: evictions/sec — what threshold is concerning?
[07:21] Samir: depends, but sustained evictions > 0.5/sec per GPU could indicate thrashing. short bursts are okay if the hit-rate recovers.
[07:33] Jules: do you have a recommended starting config for our traffic? we have median request length ~ 64 tokens, 95p ~ 512, bursts up to 200 RPS.
[07:45] Samir: starting point: continuous_batching=true, max_num_seqs=48, batch_token_ceiling=8192 (adjusts with avg tokens), token_limit_per_request=2048, priority_window_ms=30-50. KV prefetch top 200 prefixes and kv_ttl 15min. These are baseline — we'll refine after bench.
[08:08] Anika: 48 max seqs seems high compared to our previous 16. won't that increase latency?
[08:12] Samir: yes if all traffic is directed to that lane. but combined with priority windows and token_limit_per_request you keep interactive short requests out of the slow lane. think of the high throughput lane as reserved for mid-length batchable requests.
[08:29] [08:29] Maya: also, consider adaptive max_num_seqs — scale the number based on current queue depth and token mix. we have a governor that can shrink the effective max when tail latency spikes.
[08:44] Carlos: governor — is that automatic?
[08:47] Samir: yes it's an adaptive controller — it uses signals like queue length, observed p99 and GPU backlog to tweak max_num_seqs. recommended to enable it in prod with conservative bounds: min 8, max 64 for your hardware.
[09:03] Anika: if we enable the governor, do we lose deterministic throughput?
[09:07] Samir: throughput becomes more adaptive; worst-case you might see slightly lower peak throughput but much more stable tail latency. for customer-facing apps we prefer stable tails.
[09:19] Jules: about VPC/on-prem — we need to validate network egress and auditing, and also whether prefetch uses host memory that needs KMS access.
[09:30] Maya: for Private deployments we provide a control plane that can integrate with your KMS/HSM. KV prefetch doesn't require external network once the model is loaded, but audit logs and tenant metadata will flow to the control plane depending on your deployment configuration. we'll share docs.
[09:46] Carlos: one more infra question — when pinning GPUs in Dedicated, does prefetch always land on GPU memory or can it be host-resident? we want to avoid OOMs.
[09:58] Samir: configurable. in on-prem/Dedicated you can set kv_storage_preference: GPU>host or host>GPU. if GPU memory is limited, keep KV on host and ensure high-bandwidth RDMA paths. performance will be lower but more predictable.
[10:18] Anika: can we do partial prefetch — keep only first N layers' KV in GPU and rest on host?
[10:24] Samir: yes some teams do partial prefix caching — top-k layers in GPU for immediate decoder speed, lower layers on host. it's a fine-grained knob but needs tuning per model.
[10:33] [10:33] Maya: let's drill into the stress-bench plan — Samir, can you outline the test matrix?
[10:38] Samir: sure. baseline: current production config (we'll run 30m). experiment matrix: 1) continuous_batching on vs off, 2) max_num_seqs values [16,32,48,64], 3) token_limit_per_request [1024,2048,4096], 4) KV prefetch lists [none, top100, top500], 5) quantized variant at 4-bit for 10% traffic. each run ~30-60m, collect p50/p95/p99 tokens/sec, GPU util, evictions, hit-rate. we should also run a simulated cold-start spike.
[11:09] Carlos: how many hours will that be?
[11:11] Samir: roughly 8-12 hours of cluster time including repeats; we can parallelize some runs on separate pools.
[11:19] Anika: costs — that's okay if we see clear wins.
[11:23] Jules: we also need to verify fallbacks — if KV hit-rate drops, can the system gracefully route to a smaller model?
[11:31] Samir: yes we have automatic fallback policies: route to smaller variant on overload or cold starts. we recommend canary test.
[11:39] Anika: any gotchas for token limits? we've had user complaints when truncation happens unexpectedly.
[11:44] Samir: token_limit_per_request should be higher than expected user input; use server-side validation to surface truncation warnings. also prefer soft-trim (truncate with a warning token) rather than hard errors.
[11:58] [11:58] Speaker label: sometimes shows random numbers
[12:02] Maya: small demo — Samir, do you want to show the knob config snippet?
[12:06] Samir: yep — paste-coming. (short pause) okay snippet:
[12:11] "scheduler": {
[12:13]   "continuous_batching": true,
[12:15]   "max_num_seqs": 48,
[12:17]   "batch_token_ceiling": 8192,
[12:19]   "token_limit_per_request": 2048,
[12:21]   "priority_window_ms": 40,
[12:23]   "kv_prefetch_list": ["/prefixes/top-200"],
[12:25]   "kv_ttl_min": 900,
[12:26]   "eviction_policy": "lfu",
[12:28]   "governor": {"enabled": true, "min_seqs": 8, "max_seqs": 64}
[12:33] }
[12:35] Anika: that looks reasonable. can governor change max_num_seqs above 64?
[12:39] Samir: no, governor respects configured bounds.
[12:42] Carlos: when you do kv_prefetch_list is that a static list or dynamic from traces?
[12:47] Samir: can be either — static for top prefixes or dynamically generated from request traces (we provide a tool to compute top-k prefixes). dynamic prefetch generally works better.
[12:57] Anika: what's LFU vs LRU tradeoff for eviction? we have long-tail prefixes.
[13:03] Samir: LFU retains frequently used prefixes — good for stable repeated prompts. LRU keeps most recently used — better if access patterns shift quickly. for you, with morning stable patterns, LFU + TTL works well.
[13:17] Jules: about monitoring — can we get token-level billing and per-route dashboards?
[13:22] Maya: yes Console has per-route token breakdowns, latency, costs and per-token cost estimates. we'll set up a dashboard for your routes.
[13:31] Anika: any transcription mistakes in this call? (laughs)
[13:35] [13:35] small chuckle
[13:38] Carlos: one more question — how do you guard against a single client flooding with many short requests that game the priority window?
[13:46] Samir: couple measures: per-client token_limit and request-rate caps; you can also enforce fair-queueing in the scheduler to prevent one client from occupying the low-latency lane.
[13:58] Anika: okay makes sense.
